briefs.premise: A mattress warehouse whose every sale is the final sale, ending this weekend for the ninth consecutive year. Larry personally tests each mattress by napping on it, which is why the store opens late.
briefs.tone: shouty local pitchman, slowly losing his voice
briefs.structure: hard sell with a countdown to the end of the sale that keeps getting extended

briefs.premise: A third-generation repair shop that refuses to accept umbrellas are disposable. They have fixed the same umbrella for one customer since 1974 and consider it family.
briefs.structure: one long-time customer's testimonial, then the shop's address

briefs.premise: A subscription room in a strip mall that contains nothing. You pay to sit in it. An Extra Quiet tier is now available, which is the same room with the lights off.
briefs.structure: soft sell, every line a little quieter than the last

briefs.premise: A repair service that fixes your garage door and then listens to you talk about it. The doors are usually fine. It is the owners who need tuning.
briefs.structure: two voices: a customer confessing and Gary reassuring

briefs.premise: A retirement community built entirely around one enormous smoker. The brochure lists many amenities and every amenity is brisket.
briefs.tone: golden-years soft focus with a country twang
briefs.structure: three short resident testimonials in a row

briefs.premise: Accredited nap coaching for adults, with regional tournaments and a hall of fame. The head instructor is asleep for the duration of the ad.
briefs.structure: announcer hype with one student who nods off mid-sentence

briefs.premise: The town lets you adopt a pothole, name it, and receive quarterly updates on its growth. Adoption is popular. Repair is not on the roadmap.
briefs.structure: PSA with a 555 hotline and a 'this message paid for by' tag

briefs.premise: A salon promising that any haircut can be undone within twenty-four hours. The procedure is proprietary and the fine print is longer than the appointment.
briefs.structure: a short glamorous pitch, then a legal disclaimer that runs away with the spot

briefs.premise: The only store in three counties that sells nothing but ladders. Mel takes it personally when someone buys a step stool elsewhere and would like to discuss it.
briefs.tone: gruff, loyal, small-town proud, a little hurt
briefs.structure: the owner talking straight to the listener, grievance included

briefs.premise: A tiny airport with exactly one flight a day. The destination is decided each morning by the pilot's mood, and the terminal has a vending machine and a cat.
briefs.structure: jingle first, then today's surprise destination announced like a prize

briefs.premise: Balloons, streamers, and cake toppers rescued from parties that ended early. Everything is seventy percent off and thirty percent confetti.
briefs.structure: rapid-fire price list with one item that is clearly still damp

briefs.premise: Boat tours guaranteed to see nothing at all. The fog is the attraction. Full refund if visibility improves.
briefs.tone: mysterious, maritime, foghorn between the lines
briefs.structure: atmospheric narration, then the price, then the foghorn

briefs.premise: A bakery whose bread is so fresh it is technically still baking when you buy it. Oven mitts are sold separately and strongly encouraged.
briefs.structure: two voices: the announcer keeps getting interrupted by Aunt Ruthie

briefs.premise: A laboratory that reunites single socks with their partners using science. Results are not guaranteed. A support group for the unmatched meets on Thursdays.
briefs.structure: problem, solution, and a 'consult your drawer' disclaimer

briefs.premise: Amateur motorsport held entirely in one cul-de-sac. A lap takes eleven seconds, the neighbours are the sponsors, and the trophy is a lawn chair.
briefs.structure: event promo with date, time, and a 'Sunday, Sunday, Sunday' cadence

briefs.premise: A fence the cat cannot see and also does not respect. The brothers remain optimistic and offer a free second consultation, which the cat also ignores.
briefs.structure: before-and-after testimonial from a customer who is not convinced

briefs.premise: Someone comes to your house at two in the morning and quietly does the dishes. You never see them. The plates are simply clean by sunrise.
briefs.structure: soft sell that ends with a firm instruction not to wait up

briefs.premise: A forecasting hotline run by a retired man who looks out of his window. Accuracy is competitive with the professionals and the hold music is him humming.
briefs.structure: a farmer's testimonial, then the 555 hotline read very slowly

briefs.brand: The Tremont Museum of Things That Are Probably Fine
briefs.premise: A museum of objects that were once reported as concerning and turned out to be fine. Admission includes a reassuring pamphlet and a cup of lukewarm tea.
briefs.structure: docent-style narration with a members' discount at the end

briefs.premise: Trombone instruction for adults who never told their families they wanted to learn. Lessons take place in a soundproof van that parks around the corner.
briefs.structure: announcer plus one whispered testimonial from a satisfied student

briefs.premise: Twenty-four-hour casserole delivery for social emergencies: new neighbours, awkward potlucks, a cousin who showed up early. The tuna noodle is always on standby.
briefs.structure: PSA shape with a hotline and a list of covered emergencies

briefs.premise: Every tool in the store is left-handed, including the ones where that makes no sense. The tape measure is left-handed. The bucket is left-handed.
briefs.structure: a pitch whose product list escalates until it stops making sense

briefs.premise: Lifeguard certification on a pond that is eleven inches deep. Graduates are extremely confident and have never once been needed.
briefs.tone: motivational boot camp, drill sergeant energy
briefs.structure: drill-sergeant pitch with a 555 number barked at the end

briefs.premise: A lawn service that mows with scissors so as not to wake anyone. A half-acre takes about a week and the results are immaculate and quiet.
briefs.structure: soft sell read like a bedtime story

briefs.premise: A bed and breakfast with a ghost who is polite, mostly does the laundry, and would very much like a good review. Breakfast is at eight. The ghost is at nine.
briefs.structure: two voices: the innkeeper and the ghost, who is trying to help

briefs.premise: Season tickets for a theatre whose productions run long because the cast keeps adding scenes. Intermission has a buffet and, some nights, a second intermission.
briefs.structure: season promo listing shows with increasingly alarming running times

briefs.premise: Tuxedos and gowns for dogs attending events with a dress code. Alterations while you wait. The dogs do not care and look magnificent.
briefs.structure: fashion-show narration, then prices, then a dog barking once

briefs.brand: Barnaby & Sons Moving, One Lamp at a Time
briefs.premise: A moving company whose truck holds exactly one lamp. They make a great many trips and are relentlessly cheerful about every single one.
briefs.tone: upbeat, can-do, slightly out of breath
briefs.structure: two voices: the two movers finishing each other's sentences

briefs.premise: One business, two services: skate a lap while they do your return. Refunds are both literal and figurative and the Zamboni is also an accountant.
briefs.structure: jingle first, then the 'two great services' pitch

briefs.brand: The Wexley Correspondence Course in Small Talk
briefs.premise: A mail-order course covering the weather, local sports, and how about that traffic. Certificates are suitable for framing and for mentioning at parties.
briefs.structure: pitch with one sample lesson read aloud, very formally
